characterList.name: Keiichi Matsuda

content_metadata.description: A short film showcasing designer and filmmaker Keiichi Matsuda's vision for the future of augmented reality, focusing on its potential transformation of city living, transportation, and personal experiences, along with a promotion of the Dezeen and MINI Frontiers Exhibition.

qAndA.answer: He describes how users could subscribe to different layers or feeds within the augmented city, tailoring the information and experiences they see based on their interests.
qAndA.question: What specific example does Keiichi give of how augmented reality can be customized?

qAndA.answer: The project is called 'Hyper-Reality: A New Vision of the Future.' It successfully raised £29,386, exceeding its goal of £25,000.
qAndA.question: What is the title of Keiichi's Kickstarter project, and how much funding did it raise?

qAndA.answer: It will focus on both the in-car functionality (what the dashboard of the future might look like) and what happens outside the car, particularly how augmented reality can transform transportation infrastructure.
qAndA.question: What are the two main aspects of the driving experience that Keiichi's Dezeen and MINI Frontiers project will explore?

qAndA.answer: He mentions road markings, signage, and traffic systems as elements that could be adapted and enhanced using augmented reality.
qAndA.question: What specific examples does Keiichi give of everyday things that could be digitized and augmented in a future city?

qAndA.answer: He highlights contact lenses and retinal projection as possibilities for more immersive and seamless augmented reality experiences.
qAndA.question: Besides Google Glass, what other technologies does Keiichi mention as potential future interfaces for augmented reality?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, my name is Kei Chimantuda, I'm a designer and filmmaker and this is my studio in Hackney
Wake in East London.
When I was studying my masters at the Bartlett School, I started to think about how we could
introduce virtual worlds into physical spaces and that's when I found out about augmented
reality.
So I produced a series of concept films called augmented hyper reality that speculated
on how our environments could be adapted digitally and enhanced by having this ever present
overlay on the city.
One of the defining characteristics of augmented reality is that it's subjective.
I eat like everybody can see their own version of the city and it means that everything
is customizable.
So if you imagine a city is a series of layers or a series of feeds, you'd be able to
subscribe to just the ones that you like so the city itself becomes a reflection of
your taste and interests.
Since the time I started developing those original films I've always wanted to extend those
ideas and continue the research and now I've just started a self-initiated project that
I've backed on Kickstarter called hyper reality which is a series of three films each from
the perspective of a different person set in Medigene, Colombia.
When I'm actually going to see the faces of these characters, it's all a shot point of
view but what I'm thinking is that you'll be able to understand a lot about the character
just by looking at those environments.
For Dazina Mini Frontiers I'm going to take a scene in one of the upcoming hyper reality
films and explore what it's like to be driving through the augmented city.
So the film is going to look at both the kind of end-car functionality, like what the dashboard
of the future might look like, but I think the main focus is going to be on what's happening
outside the car, the kind of transport infrastructure.
The type of future that I'm imagining is a future where augmented reality is everywhere,
it's a part of everything.
We don't even consider it as a technology anymore and it means that a lot of the things
that we take for granted in everyday life, like when we're navigating on the streets
that the road marking is a signage, all of that can be applied in the digital layer.
And if we consider that it means that the way traffic systems work could become much more
dynamic and much more free-flowing so you just have sort of open spaces and you drive
according to where the markings tell you to go.
The problem of the actual interface is something that I get asked about a lot, you know,
how does this technology actually work?
What is the hard apparatus that we need to see it?
I'm aware of some projects happening right at the moment which are sort of set to kind
of revolutionise this kind of process.
It's not like Google's last putting on, but it's something much bigger and much deeper.
With an overlay, you're always going to be limited.
So people are now looking into contact lenses, for example, which apparently are doing pretty
well.
And the other big thing I think is about kind of projecting directly onto your retina.
So it uses kind of system of little mini projectors that kind of point directly in.

youtube_description:
See more design and technology movies on Dezeen: www.dezeen.com/minifrontiers

London designer Keiichi Matsuda explains how augmented reality could transform the way we navigate the city in the first of our video interviews with designers participating in our Dezeen and MINI Frontiers exhibition.

"The type of future that I'm imagining is a future where augmented reality is everywhere, it's part of everything," Matsuda says. "A lot of the things we take for granted when we're navigating the streets – the road markings, the signage – all of that can be applied in the digital layer."

He continues: "If we consider that, the way traffic systems work could become much more dynamic and much more free-flowing."

Read the full story on Dezeen: www.dezeen.com/2014/06/11/keiichi-matsuda-augmented-reality-road-markings-signage-navigation-digital-layer
